messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] standar deviation calculation
messages.body_plain:
Antonela, if you have a sample of n observations, then se is the standard deviation of their mean.  So se=sd/sqrt(n), if sd is the standard deviation of the observations themselves.  When you’re estimating density, you do not have n estimates of density, so sd of density isn’t relevant.  (If you could observer density at each line – or each point – then you could think in terms of sd of density, reflecting variability of observed densities.  But when density is estimated with a common detection function model across lines or points, this is not the case.)

You could in principle estimate the density for each line or point, but in most studies, there are too few data for each line or point for this to be useful.

Steve Buckland

We have increased our library 📔 of example analyses conducted with the R library Distance.  There are 14 examples describing the analysis, interpreting output and including code.  This creates a set of templates you can tailor 🧵 to your specific needs.

The most worthwhile use of covariates in the detection function is to cope with challenges ⚔️ presented by multi-species surveys and organisms that occur in groups.  These situations are the subject of the most recently added examples.

The first addition describes a multi-species songbird survey 🐦 in which one species is poorly represented.  The analysis presented here

http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-groupsize/Remedy-size-bias-for-dolphin-surveys.html

describes a survey of dolphins in which the dolphins occur in pods as large as 5000 individuals.  The example includes group size as a covariate to alleviate the bias in estimated size of groups caused by small groups being missed at large distances.

These two new examples join the other 12 examples available at

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] convert_units
messages.body_plain:
Joaquin

Thanks for your questions and sending along your data set.  Here is a set of code to analyse your data (comments below):

library(Distance)
joaquin <- read.csv("C:\\Users\\erexs\\Downloads\\Pludo Samborombon.csv")
joaquin$Area <- 30
names(joaquin)[4] <- "size"
convert.factor <- convert_units("metre","metre","hectare")
hn <- ds(data=joaquin,
         key="hn",
         convert.units = convert.factor,
         truncation = 140)
hn.size <- ds(data=joaquin,
           key="hn",
           formula = ~size,
           convert.units = convert.factor,
           truncation = 140)
AIC(hn, hn.size)
gof_ds(hn.size)
plot(hn.size)
summary(hn.size)

Note, I've not examined the fit of the hazard rate key function to your data, I leave that for you.

I've made two modifications to your data frame:
If you express the size of your study area in hectares, then the density estimates will be presented in hectares, so line 3 of the code changes area to hectares
the ds() function is fussy about the column name for group size: it must be lower case; that's what line 4 does
this explains why the estimates you were producing did not make sense; not recognising that there were groups (because size was not recognised), the estimates you produced were abundance of groups.
Because of the variability in group size in your data, I created a model in which detection probability was a function of group size.  Comparing models with and without the group size covariate by AIC, shows detectability is influenced by group size.  Using group size as a covariate also resolves the problem of size bias, where average group size in the sampling is a positively biased estimate of average group size in the population.

I finally perform a goodness-of-fit test of the model with group size as a covariate, showing adequate fit of that model to your data.

For this analysis, the estimated number of bird groups in the study area is 40, and the average size of each group is predicted to be 3.14, leading to an estimate of birds in the study area of 126.6.

More discussion of size bias and incorporating group size in the detection function can be found on our website: http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-groupsize/Remedy-size-bias-for-dolphin-surveys.html

Hope that is helpful.

messages.body_plain:
It could be that you have something, possibly units, mis-specified.  If you count far more birds than are present, it is because you are counting the same birds repeatedly.  This can happen either because you cover each line or point multiple times or because the plots (rectangles for lines or circles for points) overlap substantially, or a combination of both.  If you are repeatedly counting the same birds for one or both these reasons, the estimates are still valid.  You have a small site – 30ha I think – you say that is 3sqkm, but I think it is 0.3sq km?  That’s a very small area, so I would have thought that there is very unlikely to be 961 birds present, so I’m guessing that you are seeing the same birds on repeat visits and/or from neighbouring lines or points?  Anyway, it’s worth checking all your units.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Joaqu’in, I think Eric directed you towards some reading to better understand the methods and how to design studies.  P=0.53 simply indicates that just over 50% of birds on your sampled plots were detected, it gives no indication at all to how many are in your study area.  In your case, it appears that either you have overlapping plots or you have sampled each one more than once.  That’s not a problem, but it explains why you popn size estimate is less than twice the number of birds you saw.  The cv is on the high side.  To understand that, you need to look at what % of the variance comes from each source.  Estimating mean group size usually does not contribute much to variance, but it seems that you have the occasional very large group, so this component of variance is likely to be unusually high.  One possibility is to decide what is the smallest group size at which you can be certain to detect the group from at least one of your lines.  Suppose that is 50.  Then exclude those from your distance sampling analysis, and simply add the total number of birds in those large groups to your abundance estimate.  You then assume this number is known exactly, so it doesn’t affect the cv.  You’ll need to assess whether this is a reasonable strategy for you.  If not, you can reduce the cv by covering lines multiple times, and combining the data into a single analysis.

Steve Buckland

Hi

I am fairly new to the application of Distance Sampling.

We use Distance Sampling to estimate population densities as a trend over time.

Up until last year we were still able to use Distance 3.5.  However, due to operating system upgrades we now have to keep up with the times and use Distance7.3.

Using last year’s data I do not seem to be able to replicate the same or similar density estimates using 7.3 as were calculated using 3.5.

Without going into the specific details at this stage I am wondering whether you have any initial thoughts on how to rectify this.

Robbie

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My colleagues and I recently completed a point transect survey of a bromeliad plant. The population occurs in high densities in a 17.6-hectare forest over difficult karst terrain. For the majority of the observations we recorded exact distances (777 obvs.) but had to use distance bins for plants we could not reach safely (307 obvs.), after 15-meter truncation. Total observations are 1084 across 51 points after truncation.  Unfortunately, the distance bins used were too large for the study organism and perform poorly on the goodness-of-fit tests. The choice of whether to use binned or exact distances has a noticeable effect on the encounter rate of clusters estimates, 21.25 vs. 15.23 respectively, and the final density estimates.

See the attached detection functions for comparison; the exact distance figure uses 1-meter bin width for the histogram. The lack of observations in the first meter of observations in the exact distance bin plot is likely due to us finding clear patches to stand while making observations to avoid trampling the plants.

Do the 'Distance' or ' mrds' R packages have the functionality to estimate the encounter rate and the detectability separately? Or is it possible to do with a custom model?  Ideally, I would like to use all observations to estimate the encounter rate and the exact distance only to estimate detectability.

In addition, I am having trouble using any hazard rate models with this data. I keep getting the  error message:

Error in dimnames(x) <- dn :
  length of 'dimnames' [2] not equal to array extent

Any suggestions? The data I am using appears to be fine.

Kind regards,
Vaughn Bodden

Hi Vaughn,

I was a bit worried when I read your wording "The choice of whether to use binned or exact distances has a noticeable effect on the encounter rate" because, in the way most people refer to it, binning should not have an impact on encounter rate. Hence, let me restate your problem to see if I got it right.

You have a total of 1084 observations, but for a subset of these, namely 307, you could not get the exact distances. You are worried because you would like to use the full information in the other 777 distances, while for the 307 distances you just know the 5 meter class it corresponds to.

If that is the case, then I suspect in practice the loss of precision by using the 3 bins is not that big (your detection function fits seem similar) but you could also try:

1. Use all the data for encounter rate, but estimate detectability just from the 777 distances, and then use the estimated detection probability as a multiplier for the 1084 observations
2. (harder because requires bespoke coding) coding your own likelihood with two types of data coming in but informing the same likelihood

Did that help?

Cheers
